findings.evidence: This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established.
findings.fix: Report the pilot data that actually shows a pattern at or near 60 days (for example, the share of eventual returns completed within that window), or drop the claim that the cutoff matches the pilot's established pattern and justify it on its own terms.
findings.violation: The 60-day cutoff is asserted to match a return-rate pattern the pilot data established, but What the Pilot Showed never reports return timing broken out by any day count, only an aggregate on-time-or-eventual rate over the full 16 months; there is no checkable evidence behind the specific 60-day figure.

findings.evidence: During a 16-month pilot at 5 branches, the on-time-or-eventual return rate... held at 94 percent (section What the Pilot Showed) versus the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending (section Addressing the Revenue Concern)
findings.fix: Pick one branch count for the pilot and use it consistently everywhere the pilot's scope is cited, or explain why the revenue analysis covers one fewer branch than the return-rate and survey analysis.
findings.location: What the Pilot Showed, paragraph 1, versus Addressing the Revenue Concern, paragraph 2
findings.violation: The artifact states the pilot ran at 5 branches in one section and refers to the four pilot branches in another, so a reader cannot check how many branches the central return-rate and revenue evidence actually covers; the two figures cannot both be the checkable count the recommendation rests on.

findings.evidence: A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding... Consortium finance records show fine revenue covered under 2 percent of the annual materials budget...
findings.fix: Add a paragraph addressing item availability or hold-queue wait times under the no-fine policy, citing whatever the pilot measured about time-to-return or hold fulfillment, or state plainly that the pilot did not measure this and the recommendation accepts that open question.
findings.violation: The artifact's own grounds measure only whether items are eventually returned (the on-time-or-eventual return rate), not how long they take to come back; removing the only incentive to return promptly, even if the eventual-return rate holds, leaves open an availability objection (patrons and holds queues waiting longer for high-demand items) that the artifact's scope exposes but never raises or answers, addressing only the revenue objection.

findings.evidence: Specifically, the recommended change eliminates overdue fines for all item types at all ten branches, replacing the current fine notices with automatic email reminders sent three, seven, and fourteen days after the due date.
findings.fix: State whether the pilot branches used this same reminder schedule (and the result reflects it) or, if the schedule is new, say so and name what licenses expecting it to perform as well as whatever the pilot branches actually did.
findings.violation: The pilot and avoidance-survey grounds support eliminating fines in general, but nothing in What the Pilot Showed or the Tri-County brief states that pilot branches used this specific three/seven/fourteen-day email reminder schedule, so the principle connecting the measured pilot outcome to this particular replacement mechanism is never stated; a reader cannot tell whether this schedule is what produced the pilot's result or an untested addition.
